title: Q1. ISBN Number Verification Based on Checksum Calculation
statement:
An ISBN-10 is a 10-character string. The first nine characters are digits and the last character is a digit or X, where X represents 10. Number the characters from right to left as d1 through d10. The ISBN is correct if d1 + 2*d2 + ... + 10*d10 is divisible by 11. Print 1 for a correct ISBN and 0 otherwise.

Constraints: the input contains exactly 10 characters and follows the ISBN-10 character rules.

Edge cases: a checksum of 10 is written as X; an ISBN beginning with 0 is valid; the checksum can be 0.

title: Q2. Lexicographically Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement
statement:
Given a string S of lowercase English letters, rearrange all its characters to form the lexicographically smallest palindrome possible. Print -1 if no palindrome can be formed.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, where n is the length of S. S contains only lowercase letters and no spaces.

Edge cases: a one-character string is already a palindrome; an even-length string must have no odd frequency; an odd-length string may have exactly one odd frequency.

title: Q3. Minimum Additions to Make Parentheses String Valid
statement:
Given a string containing only '(' and ')', insert the minimum number of parentheses at any positions so that the final string is valid. Print the minimum number of insertions.

Constraints: 0 <= n <= 1000. The string contains only '(' and ')'.

Edge cases: the empty string needs 0 insertions; a string of only opening parentheses needs n insertions; a string of only closing parentheses needs n insertions.

title: Q4. Reverse the Order of Words
statement:
Read a sentence, count its words, and print the words in reverse order. Words are maximal sequences of non-space characters. Consecutive spaces at the beginning, end, or between words do not create extra words. Print the word count on the first line and the reversed sentence on the second line.

Constraints: the sentence length is at most 1000 characters.

Edge cases: an empty or all-space sentence has 0 words and an empty reversed sentence; a one-word sentence remains unchanged.

title: Q5. Check Whether Two Strings Are Anagrams
statement:
Given two lowercase strings, print Yes if one can be rearranged to form the other; otherwise print No. The strings are anagrams only when they contain the same characters with the same frequencies.

Constraints: 1 <= length of each string <= 1000. The strings contain only lowercase English letters and no spaces.

Edge cases: strings with repeated characters must be compared by frequency; strings of different lengths cannot be anagrams; identical strings are anagrams.

title: Q6. Wave Order of a String
statement:
Given a string S, print its characters in wave order: first character, last character, second character, second-last character, and so on moving inward.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000. S contains visible non-space characters and has no spaces.

Edge cases: for an odd length, print the middle character once; for an even length, stop after the two middle characters are placed.

title: Q7. Unpack the String
statement:
The input is a compressed string in which each lowercase letter is followed by a positive decimal count. Expand every letter by its count and print the resulting string.

Constraints: 1 <= encoded length <= 1000; each count is between 1 and 100; the expanded length is at most 100000. The format is valid: letters and counts alternate.

Edge cases: a count of 1 leaves a letter once; multiple-digit counts must be read as one number; a single letter-count pair is valid.

title: Q8. Largest Odd Number in a String
statement:
Given a string representing a non-negative integer, print the largest-valued odd integer that is a non-empty contiguous substring. If no odd integer exists, print an empty string. Keep the answer as a string.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000. The input contains only decimal digits.

Edge cases: if the last digit is odd, the whole string is the answer; otherwise remove trailing even digits until an odd digit is reached; an all-even string has no answer and prints an empty string.

title: Q9. First Non-Repeating Character
statement:
Given a case-sensitive string, print the first character whose total frequency is exactly one. If every character repeats, print No non-repeating character found. The input may contain letters, digits, symbols, and spaces; read the complete line.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000 characters. Uppercase and lowercase characters are different.

Edge cases: the first character can be the answer; a space is a valid character; if all characters repeat, print the required message.

title: Q10. Backward-4 Alphabet Cipher
statement:
In the vibrant lanes of Old Delhi, during the days of handwritten letters and secret messages, a famous storyteller named Amar would send his epic tales to trusted friends across India. To ensure that rival factions did not intercept his messages, Amar devised a simple yet clever encryption method inspired by the ancient art of Akshara (letters).

Amar's method uses a Dilli Cipher that shifts each letter by 4 positions backward in the alphabet. Write a C program that reads one complete message and encrypts it using this fixed shift.

Encryption rules:
- For uppercase letters ('A'-'Z'), shift the letter backward by 4 positions. If the shift goes before 'A', wrap around to the end of the uppercase alphabet. For example, 'A' becomes 'W', 'B' becomes 'X', 'C' becomes 'Y', and 'D' becomes 'Z'.
- For lowercase letters ('a'-'z'), shift the letter backward by 4 positions similarly. For example, 'a' becomes 'w', 'b' becomes 'x', 'c' becomes 'y', and 'd' becomes 'z'.
- Non-alphabetic characters, including spaces, digits, and punctuation marks, remain unchanged.

Input Format:
Read one line containing Amar's message. The newline marks the end of the message and is not part of the message.

Output Format:
Print the encrypted message on one line.

Example:
Input: Namaste Dilli!
Output: Jwi_opa Zehhe!

Constraints: the message length is at most 1000 characters.

Edge cases: an empty line is valid; uppercase and lowercase letters wrap independently; non-alphabetic characters remain unchanged.
